claims.text: HfNbTaTiZr is a quinary refractory concentrated or high-entropy alloy.
The target material is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The oxygen-bearing HfNbTaTiZr material is single phase.
Controlled processing can produce this material with minimal porosity and a uniform microstructure.
The proposed approach treats phonon and electron heat-transport subpopulations separately.
The approach combines ab initio electronic transport with atomistic simulations that explicitly include oxygen defects.
The predictive applicability range is 200–1200 K, provided that the microstructure remains stable without significant secondary phases.
The HfNbTaTiZr matrix has a BCC-like solid-solution structure.
The multi-principal-element distribution creates local site distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Interstitial oxygen atoms create additional local structural distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
The local distortions scatter phonons and electrons differently.
Separately tracking phonon and electron scattering captures oxygen-related energy-dissipation channels more accurately than Debye-based or perfect-crystal approximations.
The proposed approach will predict total thermal conductivity within ±15% of measurements from 200 to 1200 K.
Predicted lattice and electronic conductivity components will each remain within ±15% of measured values over 200–1200 K.
The proposed approach will improve predictive accuracy by 10–20% relative to earlier analytical estimates.
Earlier perfect-crystal or Debye-based estimates often differ from experiment by 20–30%.
Above 300 K, oxygen defects significantly influence heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
The prediction applies to similarly prepared, strain-free, single-phase HfNbTaTiZr specimens containing up to approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Observational data separately resolving phonon and electron heat flows in oxygen-bearing refractory high-entropy alloys are limited at low and high temperatures.
Laser-flash, four-probe resistivity, and Seebeck measurements can provide a decisive partition of thermal conductivity into lattice and electronic components.
